apps/perplexity/main.cpp.reason: Prefill chunk default raised from 1024 to 8192. Measured on this machine, same artifact and case, one flag apart: chunk 1024 prefills a 64,509-token prompt in 9,379.28 ms and chunk 8192 in 6,649.49 ms (-29.1%), and at 8,192-token depth 662.82 ms against 510.50 ms (-23%). The price is workspace: runtime 10.1 GiB at 1,024 against 10.6 GiB at 8,192 at the 262,144-token window, i.e. +0.5 GiB. Above 8,192 is not worth it and was tested: chunk 16384 buys 0.02% for +1.3 GiB, and chunk 32768 cannot start beside that window at all (the engine refuses with 'minimum Engine runtime reservation requires 15,412,082,945 bytes in addition to'). The field's small-chunk default exists to protect inter-token latency against concurrent decode; this product ships --max-concurrency 1 as an invariant, so that rationale is inert here while the cost is not. The two EnginePurpose::CausalScoring overrides that also set 1024 are deliberately untouched -- they are purpose-specific configurations that pin concurrency, drop speculation and disable vision, not stale copies of this default.

apps/serve/main.cpp.reason: Engine-failure reporting: the engine latches failure permanently (fail_all_locked sets failed_ once and nothing clears it), so without this check the process stays alive forever after an engine-wide failure, indistinguishable from a healthy one at the process level. The failure is state released that was not held, which needs several lanes active at once and a cache serving a shared prefix. Its first end-to-end run, 2026-10-06, found two things the case could not have revealed before it ran: `_assistant()` was called with one argument where it takes two, so the run failed with `TypeError: _assistant() missing 1 required positional argument: 'handle'` before round 2; and the comment claiming 60 rounds take each lane past 8,000 tokens was an assumption -- the run measured 2,078 -> 5,804 (lane a). Both corrected in place; the workload was left alone because that run is the case's first recorded baseline. 2026-10-08: the cancellation requirement relaxed to the contract its own layer's tests pin. `_require_transport_cancellation` demanded `http.cancelled`, but `execution.py:501` derives that from the client transport and `test_http_cancellation.py:112,144` assert `cancel_requested` with `transport_cancelled` False as a VALID state after a cancellation -- so cancel-before-first and cancel-after-first could never pass, and had never been run to notice. The requirement now accepts either cancellation-shaped outcome and still demands that the cancellation was requested, that no protocol terminal arrived, and that the request completed.
